title: Project I
text: Project I Since the beginning of our National Center for Translational Research in Reproduction & Infertility in 2019, our knowledge of genetic causes of infertility has expanded dramatically. In a recent (2022) study of whole-exome sequencing (WES) from 1,000 cases of unexplained male infertility, we identified a plausible monogenic cause in 20% of cases. Similar diagnostic yields have been reported for other male infertility cohorts. Despite these impressive research advances, there are two major shortcomings of our work. First, we are not identifying all genetic causes in our patients. Second, even though we understand the genetics much better than 5 years ago, we have not made any impact on clinical diagnosis. In this proposal, our goal is to improve the diagnostic yield of clinical genome sequencing for male infertility in two ways. First, we aim to improve diagnostic yield with new approaches to sequencing and interpretation of genomes of male infertility. We will transition from WES to whole genome sequencing (WGS), and in the process, expand our analysis methods to new types of variants detectable by WGS. We will expand our analysis to new disease models for which we have been historically underpowered to capture, such as autosomal dominant and digenic, and to interrogate genes involved in testis development which have been previously overlooked. These new approaches will be applied to our existing database of >1,600 WES data from patients, >80% of which are still unsolved, and to new patients that we continue to enroll. Second, we aim to improve translation of our research findings by organizing an international clinical genetics community to generate and share gene and variant interpretations. In the modern clinical genetics landscape, most diagnostic workflows rely heavily on published guidelines for the interpretation of genetic variants. Notably, there are no official expert panels reviewing genes or variants for infertility. We will reactivate our existing international team, which has performed gene and variant interpretation in 2018 and 2020, to fill this gap. We will build open our expertise and accelerate our curation by creating a shared online working environment that records and reconciles interpretations. This review environment will also provide reference information on testis gene expression, fertility phenotypes of mutations across multiple model organisms, and an allele frequency database built from over 1,000 genomes of male infertility cases and 600 genomes from normozoospermic controls. At the end of this 5-year project, we believe we will have achieved a milestone that we targeted over 10 years ago. We will have built a strong foundation of solid research in male infertility genetics, summarized and packaged this knowledge for clinical use. We aspire that, in 2029, genome sequencing will finally become a routine clinical test for the diagnosis of male infertility.

title: Neuronal-Glial Coupling Mechanisms in Temporomandibular Joint Pain
text:
Temporomandibular disorders (TMD) are a leading cause of chronic orofacial pain, significantly
impacting quality of life and public health. In this proposal, we investigate the mechanisms
underlying TMD pain within the trigeminal ganglia at the molecular, cellular, and behavioral levels
using a combination of state-of-the-art approaches. By examining the role of connexin 43 (Cx43)-
mediated gap junction coupling in maladaptive neuronal plasticity and chronic pain, this research
will provide fundamental insights into TMD pathophysiology and identify therapeutic targets to
guide the development of mechanism-based interventions, ultimately reducing disability and
improving patient outcomes.

title: Methods for measuring matrisome molecule similarity during disease processes
text:
The matrisome consists of glycosylated extracellular matrix and cell surface proteins that surround cells and
support normal physiological activity. While it is known that glycosylation changes during disease processes, it
has not been possible to quantitatively compare glycoprotein structure among biological samples. We aim to
develop technologies to meet this need.

title: Center for Translational Viral Oncology (CTVO)
text: Phase 2 of the “Center for Translational Viral Oncology” (CTVO) will leverage success of Phase 1coupled to evolving research themes that incorporate new faculty that address virus-induced malignancies occurring at high incidence in our region. These cancers are highly prevalent in Louisiana and occur at increased incidence in people living with HIV. The overarching goal of CTVO is to improve disease management and quality of life across Louisiana patients through responsive research activity including the following 1) sustaining the career development of talented Junior Principal Investigators (JPIs) 2) supporting existing and coalescing research between regional scientists in viral oncology and 3) reinforcing the institutionalization of productive core facilities.

title: XERO study: A Phase I study of CVGN8 for the treatment of Radiation-Induced Xerostomia
text:
A side effect of radiation for head and neck cancer is damage to the salivary glands, leaving patients with lifelong
dry mouth (xerostomia) that causes pain, difficulty eating, and reduced quality of life. Current treatments only
ease symptoms temporarily and do not repair the damaged glands. This grant will support the planning and first
clinical trial of a new injectable therapy, CVGN8, designed to regenerate the salivary glands and restore saliva
production in order to meaningfully improve dry mouth for cancer survivors.

title: Ion coupling, permeation, and regulation in glutamate transporters
text:
Glutamate is a neurotransmitter in the brain that mediates cognition, memory, and learning; specialized proteins,
called glutamate transporters, regulate the amount and movements of glutamate in the brain in processes
controlled by ions. This proposal aims to understand how these transporters evolved to perform their essential
functions and how they interact with ions in health and disease.

title: ROLE OF LET-7/EZH2/BACH1 DOUBLE NEGATIVE FEEDBACK LOOP IN AT1/AT2 CELL INDUCED ILD
text:
The proposed research is fundamental to our understanding of the contribution of regulatory class
microRNAs on alveolar type 1 (AT1) and alveolar type 2 (AT2) epithelial cell homeostasis and interstitial
lung disease. Proposed studies can lead to new microRNA targeted therapies aimed at improving
AT1/AT2 cell function and cell survival, ultimately protecting patients from lung fibrosis.

title: Targeted Prodrug Cytokines for Metastatic Breast Cancer Immunotherapy
text:
Project Narrative.
There is an unmet clinical need for mBC treatment options, which are highly limited due to the anatomical,
physiological, and biological factors of targeting multiple sites at once without compromising patient quality of
life, challenges faced during high-risk surgery for permanent damage to critical brain structures, and limitations
of targeted therapies to penetrate the blood-brain barrier (BBB). An ideal less-invasive breast cancer therapy
would offer direct access to primary and secondary tumors to improve the delivery specificity of an
immunotherapy that harnesses the patient’s immune system to reduce tumor burden and generate long-lasting
immunological memory, without leading to off-target toxicity effects after treatment, or a reduction in patient
quality of life. In this project, we will develop an innovative breast cancer therapy to deliver immunomodulatory
agents – specifically, protein cytokines – to both the primary tumor and across the BBB to secondary tumors to
reshape the TME and treat metastatic breast cancer without systemic toxicities.

title: PPARalpha activation underlies sex dimorphism in chemotherapy-induced cardiotoxicity
text:
.
Cardiotoxicity of anti-cancer chemotherapy is becoming increasingly prevalent due to advances in treating
cancers and diminishing patients’ health and lifespan, however, effective cardioprotective strategies are still not
available. This proposal aims to identify the mechanisms that promote sex-specific cardiotoxicity in mouse and
human hearts and therefore, to identify therapeutic targets for sex-specific cardioprotective treatment. We will
focus on the role of PPARα, the regulator of fatty acid metabolism in the heart, as a potential target for sex-
specific cardioprotection during chemotherapy.

title: A Novel RAD51-BRCA2 Complex Stabilizing Drug: A Medical Countermeasure for Mitigating Accidental Radiation Exposure
text:
Accidental radiation exposure poses serious risks to human health, causing both immediate and long-term harm.
This proposal investigates the effectiveness of our newly developed small molecule, designed to target proteins
involved in radiation-induced DNA repair, in mitigating mortality and alleviating long-term toxicity in preclinical
animal models exposed to lethal whole-body radiation. The potential impact of these findings goes beyond
immediate mitigation, offering substantial contributions to the development of a potent and safe medical
countermeasure agent for the effective mitigation of long-term health risks associated with accidental radiation
exposure.

title: Technologies to enable safe and effective gene editing in skeletal muscle
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health as it develops enabling technologies for gene editing in
skeletal muscle. Current rates of gene editing in this tissue are low and methods are lacking for how to control
expression of gene editing enzymes in this tissue. We will develop new technologies to 1) edit as many
myonuclei as possible in the context of the myofiber syncytia, 2) control expression of gene editing enzymes,
and 3) integrate these elements into a single gene therapy vector.

title: Targeting Intracellular CD38 to Reduce Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury in Liver Transplantation
text:
Organs from donation after cardiac death (DCD) donors represent the greatest opportunity to expand the donor
pool and make liver transplantation more accessible. Paradoxically, the organs we most need to expand access
are also the ones most likely to harm the recipient due to the substantial warm ischemic injury present at
procurement. Our studies will characterize and test the therapeutic benefit of inhibiting the multifunctional
inflammatory enzyme CD38, particularly type III CD38, to preserve donor organ integrity and rescue function
during DCD liver transplantation.

title: Imaging Structure and Function Core
text: Imaging technologies such as confocal microscopy, multiphoton microscopy as well as optical coherence tomography and adaptive optics have transformed the ability of scientists to observe structural and functional changes in the visual system, in vivo and ex vivo, in both health and disease. The overarching goal of the imaging core is to transform the ability of vision scientists to use these critical technologies by providing access to and training on the newest imaging modalities, and transferring novel approaches between groups to facilitate innovation in research and collaboration across vision research disciplines. This goal will be achieved through supporting (1) access to new confocal and OCT/in vivo fluorescence microscopes as well as custom adaptive optics imaging ophthalmoscopes that will be made available through the Ophthalmology Department, (2) access to advanced imaging modalities available through various Stanford Microscopy Facilities, and (3) development, application and dissemination of customized in vivo imaging approaches and systems developed by investigators in the vision research center.

title: The Meharry Research Training Initiative
text: This project supports a comprehensive training program at Meharry Medical College that prepares graduate students for careers in biomedical research. Through mentorship rigorous coursework and career development, trainees will gain the skills needed to succeed in a variety of scientific fields thereby strengthening the national biomedical research workforce.

title: In Vitro Identification of miR-718 targets and miR-718-induced epigenetic modifications
text:
MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are critical regulators of gene expression and may be causative factors in disease
development. This study will examine what genes are targeted by increased levels of an understudied miRNA-
miR-718- and the relationship of these gene targets to changes in epigenetics in a human neuronal cell line.

title: Dynamic changes in PIP2 binding sites and their impact on axonal targeting and function of epilepsy-associated KCNQ/Kv7 channels
text:
Voltage-gated Kv7/KCNQ potassium channels require membrane lipid cofactor PIP2 to open and calmodulin
to traffic to the neuronal axons where they potently suppress repetitive and burst firing of action potentials.
This proposal will identify the PIP2 binding sites that change by different gating states, subunit composition,
and calmodulin binding of Kv7 channels, thereby controlling their axonal enrichment and function to reduce
neuronal excitability. In contrast to a well-established role of PIP2 in gating modulation, this project will
provide novel concepts that the PIP2 binding landscape is dynamic and modulates both function and
trafficking of axonal Kv7 channels to impact neuronal excitability and the mechanisms of pathogenic variants
in Kv7 subunits that cause epilepsy.

title: Sex-dependent shifts in behavioral profiles and cortical signaling following adolescent binge drinking
text:
Adolescent alcohol exposure has profound effects on brain development and adulthood substance misuse, but
the neuroadaptations that drive sex-dependent susceptibility and resiliency in response to adolescent drinking
remain unknown. Our project aims to address this gap by using advanced technologies and well-founded
methods to launch a hypothesis-driven investigation into the involvement of a specific population of neurons
(SST neurons), their interactions with sex hormones, and how this system is altered at multiple time points post-
adolescent alcohol exposure. This work will provide key insights into the neurobiological underpinnings of
adolescent binge drinking—a major public health problem and precursor to adulthood alcohol use disorder
(AUD).

title: Elucidating roles of APC-specific pMHC patterning
text:
T cells are regulated through interactions with many types of antigen-presenting cells (APCs) that can each
program a T cell's functionality in various ways, but the underlying mechanisms of how different APCs induce
such varied responses in T cells is not understood. I will apply cutting-edge high-resolution imaging
approaches to define how peptide-MHC patterning on APCs underlies their ability to regulate T cell activity and
modulate peptide-MHC surface patterns in vivo to generate productive APC-T cell interactions for targeting
tumor cells. This study will add a significant, novel layer to our understanding of regulators of T cell activation
through dissection of APC properties and nominate a strategy to therapeutically harness these findings in
immunologic diseases.

title: Oscillatory Recurrent Gated Neural Integrator Circuits (ORGaNICs): a unified framework for neural dynamics and human cognition
text:
There is increasing recognition that many neurological and psychiatric illnesses are dysfunctions of neural
circuit computation. But we lack a theoretical framework for how such neural circuit computations function to
support a wide variety of cognitive processes. Through the proposed research, we aim to provide such a
theory, thereby providing a better understanding of the details of how brain circuits operate, leading to better
assessment, diagnosis, and treatment of a wide range of brain disorders.

title: Reproductive tract organ development and differentiation
text:
The proposed studies will provide basic knowledge of the molecular, cellular, and developmental mechanisms
of uterus formation and the gene expression mechanisms that mediate the hormone pathway for the
elimination of female reproductive tract organ progenitor tissues during male differentiation. These studies
should provide new insights into the causes of uterine variation and sex development.
